summary: Sets out terminology and requirements for the Drone Remote Identification Protocol working group. The goal is to support remote identification and tracking of unmanned aircraft for safety and security, using existing Internet resources. It also covers making identification information verifiable as trustworthy, both online and offline. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9153 sets requirements for systems that identify unmanned aircraft during flight. It calls for ways to check that an aircraft's identity and related messages are trustworthy, even when an observer has no Internet connection.

subtitle: Terminology and requirements for trustworthy drone remote identification.

tldr.problem: Remote identification can help observers identify unmanned aircraft, but broadcast links are short, one-way, and may work without Internet access. Existing messages can assert an identity without proving that the sender owns it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9153 defines terminology and requirements for a family of DRIP protocols, including offline-verifiable ownership and registration, binding related messages to an identifier, and protections for private information.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC sets requirements and terminology; it does not define the DRIP protocols that satisfy them. It points to a companion architecture and other DRIP documents for solution details.

today: RFC 9153 is an Informational requirements and terminology document. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Remote Identification Needs Trust
sections.content:
Remote identification and tracking can help observers identify unmanned aircraft and support safety, security, and related services. The RFC describes constraints that make this difficult: small aircraft have limited power and space, radio links can be unreliable, and an observer or aircraft may lack Internet access.

RFC 9153 defines requirements and common terms for the Drone Remote Identification Protocol (DRIP) Working Group. It does not specify a protocol. It says that a companion architecture document and other DRIP documents describe ways to meet the requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Observers need to know which unmanned aircraft they are seeing and whether its reported identity is trustworthy. This RFC lists requirements for systems that provide that information under difficult connectivity and device limits.

sections.title: Network RID and Broadcast RID
sections.content:
The RFC describes two remote-identification methods from ASTM F3411-19. Network RID makes information available through Internet-connected servers that observers can query. Broadcast RID sends messages one-way over a local radio link, directly from an aircraft to nearby observer devices, without IP between the radio link and application.

Broadcast RID can work without Internet access, but the observer may need Internet access for registry lookup or a verification service. The RFC explains that the basic identifier message does not prove that the sender owns the identifier, and that the standard's authentication message provides framing but does not specify an authentication method. Its constrained message size also limits what authentication information can be sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Network RID uses servers that observers reach over the Internet. Broadcast RID sends information directly to nearby devices, but the message needs additional means to prove who sent it.

sections.title: General and Registry Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements apply to DRIP as a set of related protocols; each protocol does not have to satisfy every requirement by itself. General requirements include checking that an identifier belongs to the current sender, binding other remote-identification messages to that identifier, and checking that the identifier is registered. These checks must be possible on an observer device without Internet access at the time of observation.

Other requirements cover readable information, gateways that can record when and where they received a broadcast, authenticated communications when connectivity permits, and policy-based performance settings. Registry requirements distinguish public information from private information and require access controls for private records.
sections.plainLanguage: The full set of DRIP protocols must make identity, message binding, and registration checkable, including offline. It must also distinguish public registry information from private information that needs access controls.

sections.title: Requirements for DRIP Identifiers
sections.content:
The identifier requirements say that a DRIP Entity Identifier must identify a registry and allow information about the entity to be found there. The identifier must be unique in its global space from registration until deregistration, and it must be difficult to spoof or use to link separate operations. The maximum identifier length is 19 bytes.

The RFC distinguishes the DRIP identifier from the wider UAS ID terminology used in the remote-identification standard. It notes that the standard allows a UAS ID of up to 20 bytes, while a proposed Specific Session ID uses one byte for a subtype, leaving 19 bytes for the identifier itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A DRIP identifier must be short, unique, and linked to the registry that holds its information. It should be difficult to copy or use to connect an entity's separate operations.

sections.title: Privacy, Security and Transparency
sections.content:
The privacy requirements call for confidential handling of private information and support for selective encryption of private data while it is being sent. When private data travels over IP, encryption must be end-to-end. Safety-critical information broadcast locally must remain usable by authorized observers who are unlikely to have a way to decrypt it.

The RFC notes that public identification and private operator information can create competing needs for transparency and privacy. It identifies possible risks such as spoofed identifiers, replay, attacks on registration messages, malicious registries, and attempts to impersonate an aircraft or operator. Because the document defines requirements rather than protocols, these are considerations for later solution designs.
sections.plainLanguage: Some identification information must be available to observers, while personal information needs protection. Later protocol designs must address spoofing and other attacks without making safety information unreadable to authorized observers.
